Content:
Suppose we want to evaluate the following expression using a scientific calculator:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{e-1}]

Content:
Using parentheses when inputting the denominator [MATH: e-1] into a calculator is essential. This is because [MATH: \pi \div e - 1] is equivalent to

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\pi}e - 1]
which is not the same as the expression we want to evaluate!

Content:
So, let's begin by rewriting our expression using parentheses:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{e-1} = \pi \div \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{(}e - 1\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{)}]

Content:
We're now ready to enter this expression into a calculator. To do so, we note the following:

Content:
- We enter the symbols from left to right as they appear.
- Your calculator will have special [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,(\,}] and [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,)\,}] buttons for left and right parentheses.
- Scientific and graphing calculators usually have special [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,e\,}] and [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\pi\,}] buttons. You may need to press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\textrm{2nd}}] or [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\textrm{SHIFT}}] to access these.

Content:
Evaluating this using a calculator, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: \pi \div (e - 1) \approx 1.828]

Content:
rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to evaluate expressions on a graphing calculator.

Content:
This lesson is designed to help prepare you for the parts of the AP Calculus exam where graphing calculators are needed.

Content:
If you want to succeed on the AP Calculus exam, then you must acquire a physical graphing calculator and use it when completing this lesson.

Content:
Do not use any other type of online tool, as you will not be allowed to use it during the exam. You need to practice with the specific calculator that you will use on the AP exam so that you can solve problems quickly without wasting any time troubleshooting your calculator.

Content:
A comprehensive list of calculators that are permitted in the AP Calculus exams can be found here.

Content:
Throughout this lesson, we will list buttons that feature on a TI-84 Plus CE-T graphing calculator. We'll also mention some common alternative buttons on other calculator models.

Content:
Similar models will have the same or similar buttons, and even dissimilar models may have similar buttons.

Content:
If you have a different calculator model and cannot find the right buttons to press, the best way to resolve this is to either to

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] (a) consult your calculator's manual, or

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] (b) search online for a video that explains how to operate your calculator.

Content:
The best way to get familiar with your calculator is to consult its manual. Manuals can usually be found online. For example, a link to the manual for a TI-84 Plus CE-T can be found by entering the following query into a search engine.

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] online manual TI-84 Plus CE-T

Content:
If you have a different model calculator, replace "TI-84 Plus CE-T" in the query above with your calculator's model.

Content:
Answers to common questions can be found by searching for online videos explaining how the calculator works. For example, to find a video that shows how to use the [MATH: \pi] button on a TI-84, you might type the following query into a search engine.

Content:
[MATH: \qquad] video access the pi button on TI-84

Content:
Again, replace "TI-84" in the query above with your calculator's model. Also, bear in mind that videos for similar models might also help.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Evaluating an Expression Using a Calculator

Content:
Suppose we want to evaluate the following expression using a scientific calculator:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{e-1}]

Content:
Using parentheses when inputting the denominator [MATH: e-1] into a calculator is essential. This is because [MATH: \pi \div e - 1] is equivalent to

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\pi}e - 1]
which is not the same as the expression we want to evaluate!

Content:
So, let's begin by rewriting our expression using parentheses:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{e-1} = \pi \div \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{(}e - 1\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{)}]

Content:
We're now ready to enter this expression into a calculator. To do so, we note the following:

Content:
- We enter the symbols from left to right as they appear.
- Your calculator will have special [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,(\,}] and [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,)\,}] buttons for left and right parentheses.
- Scientific and graphing calculators usually have special [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,e\,}] and [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\pi\,}] buttons. You may need to press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\textrm{2nd}}] or [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\textrm{SHIFT}}] to access these.

Content:
Evaluating this using a calculator, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: \pi \div (e - 1) \approx 1.828]

Content:
rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

Content:
When evaluating expressions on a scientific or graphing calculator, we always round to [MATH: 3] decimal places unless stated otherwise.

---

Item 3 — Example: Using Parentheses to Evaluate Rational Expressions

Example Prompt:
Evaluate [MATH: \dfrac{e+7}{\pi-1}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that we always round to [MATH: 3] decimal places unless stated otherwise.

Our expression can be written as follows:

[MATH: \dfrac{e+7}{\pi-1} = {\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{(}e+7\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{)}} \div {\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{(}\pi-1\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{)}}]

We're now ready to enter this expression into a calculator. To do so, we note the following:

- We enter the symbols from left to right as they appear.
- Your calculator will have special [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,(\,}] and [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,)\,}] buttons for left and right parentheses.
- Scientific and graphing calculators usually have special [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,e\,}] and [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\pi\,}] buttons. You may need to press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\textrm{2nd}}] or [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\textrm{SHIFT}}] to access these.

Notice the parentheses in the expression above.

Evaluating this using a calculator, we obtain

[MATH: (e+7) \div (\pi-1) \approx 4.538]

rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

Item 6 — Tutorial: The Negative Sign Button

Content:
Scientific and graphing calculators usually have a special "negative sign" button for negative numbers. It's usually a minus sign enclosed in parentheses [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}(-)}.]

Content:
This is not the same as the "subtract" button, which is usually written as a minus sign [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,-\,}] without parentheses. Confusing the two can lead to errors.

Content:
Let's evaluate the following expression using a calculator, rounding our answer to five decimal places:

Content:
[MATH: 5^{-1-e}]

Content:
To evaluate this expression using a calculator, we note the following:

Content:
- To raise a number to a power, you need to use the [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\wedge\,}] button. On some calculators, this might be an [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,x^y\,}] button, or similar. You may need to press [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\textrm{2nd}}] or [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\textrm{SHIFT}}] to access this.
- The first number in the exponent is [MATH: -1,] so we use the "negative sign" button [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}(-)}] when entering this number.
- We then subtract [MATH: e] from [MATH: -1,] so we use the "subtract" button [MATH: \bbox[2px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,-\,}] for this operation.

Content:
Therefore, we'd use a sequence of buttons similar to the following to evaluate this expression:
[MATH: \bbox[6px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,5\,} \qquad
\bbox[6px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\land\,} \qquad
\bbox[3px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}(-)} \qquad
\bbox[6px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,1\,} \qquad
\bbox[5px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,-\,} \qquad
\bbox[7px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,e\,} \qquad
\bbox[7px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,=\,}]

Content:
Evaluating our expression using a scientific or graphing calculator, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: 5^{-1-e} \approx 0.002\,52]

Content:
rounded to [MATH: 5] decimal places.

Content:
Watch out! In the sequence of buttons above, we assume that pressing the exponent button moves the cursor upwards into a superscript. If your calculator does not do this, then it is likely necessary to enclose the exponent in parentheses:

Content:
[MATH: \bbox[6px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,5\,} \qquad
\bbox[6px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,\land\,} \qquad
\bbox[6px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,(\,} \qquad
\bbox[3px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}(-)} \qquad
\bbox[6px, border: 2px solid gray]{\color{gray}\,1\,} \qquad

Recall that we always round to [MATH: 3] decimal places unless stated otherwise.

Item 11 — Tutorial: Evaluating Radicals

Explanation:
